paragraphs: In countries where the poor *e alone hold the power to make the laws, no great economy in public spending should be expected. That spending will always be considerable, either because the taxes do not fall on those who vote them, or because they are laid in such a way as not to fall on those classes. In other words, the government of the democracy is the only kind of government in which the power that imposes taxes escapes paying them.

e [ The word poor is used here, and throughout the rest of this chapter, in a relative sense, not an absolute one. Poor men in America would often look rich beside the poor of Europe, but they may rightly be called poor in comparison with their wealthier countrymen.]

It may be objected (though the argument carries no real weight) that the true interest of the people is inseparably tied to that of the wealthier part of the community, since the people cannot help suffering from the harsh measures it adopts. But is it not in the true interest of kings to make their subjects happy, and in the true interest of nobles to admit new members into their order on reasonable terms? If distant advantages could prevail over the passions and pressures of the moment, there could never be a tyrannical sovereign or an exclusive aristocracy.

It may also be objected that the poor are never given the sole power of making the laws. I reply that wherever universal suffrage has been established, the majority of the community unquestionably holds the legislative authority. If it is shown that the poor always make up the majority, it may be added, with perfect truth, that in countries where they have the right to vote they hold the sole power of making laws. But it is certain that in every nation of the world the greater number has always consisted of people who own no property, or whose property is too small to spare them the need to work in order to live in modest comfort. Universal suffrage therefore does, in point of fact, place the government of society in the hands of the poor.

The harm that popular authority may sometimes do to the finances of a State was plainly visible in some of the democratic republics of antiquity, where the public treasury was drained to relieve needy citizens or to pay for the games and theatrical entertainments of the populace. It is true that the representative system was then very imperfectly understood, and that today popular passion is less felt in the conduct of public affairs. Still, it may be believed that the delegate will in the end conform to the principles of his constituents, and will indulge their inclinations as much as their interests.

The extravagance of democracy, however, is less to be feared the more the people acquire a share of property. On one hand, the contributions of the rich are then less needed; on the other, it is harder to lay on taxes that do not affect the interests of the lower classes. For this reason universal suffrage would be less dangerous in France than in England, because in England the property on which taxes may be levied is held by fewer hands. America, where the great majority of citizens own some fortune, is in a still more favorable position than France.

There are further causes that may increase public expenditure in democratic countries. When an aristocracy governs, the individuals who run the affairs of State are spared every kind of privation by their own place in society. They are content with their position; power and renown are what they strive for. Because they stand far above the more obscure mass of citizens, they do not always clearly see how the well-being of the people at large should add to their own honor. They are not indeed unfeeling toward the sufferings of the poor, but they cannot feel those miseries as keenly as if they shared them. As long as the people appear to accept their lot, the rulers are satisfied, and they ask nothing more of the government. An aristocracy is more concerned with how to keep its influence than with how to improve its condition.

When, on the contrary, the people hold supreme authority, the constant awareness of their own miseries drives the rulers of society to seek constant improvements. A thousand different things are put up for improvement; the most trivial details are sought out as open to amendment; and changes that involve considerable expense are especially pressed, since the aim is to make life more bearable for the poor, who cannot pay for themselves.
Moreover, all democratic communities are stirred by a vague excitement and a kind of feverish impatience, which give rise to a multitude of innovations, almost all of which cost money.

In monarchies and aristocracies, the rulers’ natural taste for power and renown is spurred on by ambition, and these temptations often push them into very costly undertakings. In democracies, where the rulers suffer privations, they can be won over only by means that improve their well-being, and such improvements cannot happen without spending money. When a people begins to reflect on its situation, it discovers a multitude of wants it had not felt before, and to satisfy these needs it must turn to the coffers of the State. Hence public charges grow as civilization spreads, and taxes are raised as knowledge pervades the community.

The last cause that often makes a democratic government dearer than any other is that a democracy does not always succeed in moderating its expenditure, because it does not understand the art of economy. Its plans are frequently changed, and the agents who carry them out are removed still more often, so its undertakings are often badly managed or left unfinished. In the first case the State spends sums out of all proportion to the goal it has set; in the second, the expense itself brings no return. *f

f [ The gross receipts of the Treasury of the United States in 1832 were about $28,000,000; in 1870 they had risen to $411,000,000. The gross expenditure in 1832 was $30,000,000; in 1870, $309,000,000.]
Tendencies of the American Democracy as Regards the Salaries of Public Officers

In democracies those who set high salaries have no chance of profiting by them — Tendency of the American democracy to raise the salaries of subordinate officers and to lower those of the more important officials — Reason for this — Comparison of the salaries of public officers in the United States and in France.

There is a powerful reason that usually leads democracies to economize on the salaries of public officers. In democratic countries the number of citizens who pay out the remuneration is extremely large, while the number of persons who can hope to benefit from receiving it is comparatively small. In aristocratic countries, on the contrary, the individuals who fix high salaries almost always have a vague hope of profiting by them. These appointments may be seen as capital they create for their own use, or at least as a resource for their children.

It must, however, be admitted that a democratic State is most stingy toward its principal agents. In America the secondary officers are much better paid, and the dignitaries of the administration much worse paid, than anywhere else.

These opposite effects result from the same cause. In both cases the people fixes the salaries of public officers, and the scale of pay is determined by the people’s own wants. It is held to be fair that the servants of the public should live in the same comfortable circumstances as the public itself; *g but when the question concerns the salaries of the great officers of State, this rule fails, and chance alone can guide the popular decision. The poor have no adequate idea of the wants the higher classes of society may feel. A sum that is scanty to the rich seems enormous to the poor man, whose wants do not go beyond the necessities of life; and in his eyes the Governor of a State, with his twelve or fifteen hundred dollars a year, is a very fortunate and enviable being. *h If you try to convince him that the representative of a great people ought to be able to keep up some show of splendor in the eyes of foreign nations, he will perhaps agree with you. But when he thinks of his own humble dwelling and the hard-earned produce of his wearisome toil, he remembers all he could do with a salary you call insufficient, and he is startled, almost frightened, at the sight of such uncommon wealth. Besides, the secondary public officer is almost on a level with the people, while the others are raised above it. The former may therefore excite his interest, but the latter begins to arouse his envy.

g [ The comfortable circumstances of secondary officials in the United States also result from another cause, which is independent of the general tendencies of democracy. Every kind of private business is very lucrative, and the State would not be served at all if it did not pay its servants well. The country is in the position of a commercial enterprise that is obliged to sustain costly competition, in spite of its taste for economy.]
h [ The State of Ohio, which has a million inhabitants, gives its Governor a salary of only $1,200 a year.]
This is very clearly seen in the United States, where salaries seem to decrease as the authority of those who receive them increases *i

i [ To make this assertion perfectly clear, it is enough to examine the scale of salaries of the agents of the Federal Government. To complete the comparison, I have added the salaries attached to the corresponding offices in France under the constitutional monarchy.

United States Treasury Department Messenger ............................   $700 Clerk with lowest salary .............  1,000 Clerk with highest salary ............  1,600 Chief Clerk ..........................  2,000 Secretary of State ...................  6,000 The President ........................ 25,000

France Ministere des Finances Hussier ........................... 1,500 fr. Clerk with lowest salary,  1,000 to 1,800 fr. Clerk with highest salary  3,200 to 8,600 fr. Secretaire-general ................20,000 fr. The Minister ......................80,000 fr. The King ......................12,000,000 fr.

I have perhaps done wrong in choosing France as my standard of comparison. In France the democratic tendencies of the nation have an ever-increasing influence on the government, and the Chambers show a disposition to raise the low salaries and lower the principal ones. Thus the Minister of Finance, who received 160,000 fr. under the Empire, receives 80,000 fr. in 1835; the Directeurs-generaux of Finance, who then received 50,000 fr., now receive only 20,000 fr. [This comparison is based on the state of things existing in France and the United States in 1831. It has since changed materially in both countries, but not so much as to undermine the truth of the author’s observation.]]

Under the rule of an aristocracy, on the contrary, it often happens that while the high officers receive munificent salaries, the inferior ones have barely enough to procure the necessities of life. The reason is easy to find, in causes very similar to those I have just mentioned. If a democracy cannot imagine the pleasures of the rich, or watch them without envy, an aristocracy is slow to understand the privations of the poor — or, to speak more correctly, knows nothing of them. The poor man is not (if we use the term properly) the fellow of the rich one; he is a being of another kind. An aristocracy is therefore apt to care little about the fate of its subordinate agents, and their salaries are raised only when they refuse to do their work for too scanty a payment.

It is the stinginess of democracy toward its principal officers that has given rise to a belief that it is far more economical than it really is. It is true that democracy scarcely allows the individuals who conduct its affairs the means of an honorable living; but enormous sums are lavished to meet the needs of the people or to make their enjoyments easier. *j The money raised by taxation may be better spent, but it is not saved. In general, democracy gives generously to the community and very sparingly to those who govern it. The reverse is the case in aristocratic countries, where the money of the State is spent for the profit of the persons at the head of affairs.

j [ See the American budgets for the cost of poor relief and free instruction. In 1831 $250,000 were spent in the State of New York for the support of the poor, and at least $1,000,000 were devoted to free instruction. (William’s “New York Annual Register,” 1832, pp. 205 and 243.) The State of New York contained only 1,900,000 inhabitants in the year 1830, which is not more than double the population of the Department du Nord in France.]
Difficulty of Distinguishing the Causes Which Contribute to the Economy of the American Government

We are liable to frequent errors in researching the facts that have a serious influence on the fate of mankind, since nothing is more difficult than to appreciate their real value. One people is naturally inconsistent and enthusiastic; another is sober and calculating. These characteristics originate in their physical constitution or in remote causes we do not know.

Some nations are fond of display and the bustle of festivity, and do not regret the costly pleasures of an hour. Others, on the contrary, are attached to quieter pleasures, and seem almost ashamed of appearing to be pleased. In some countries the highest value is set on the beauty of public buildings; in others works of art are treated with indifference, and everything unproductive is looked down on with contempt. In some, renown is the ruling passion; in others, money.

Apart from the laws, all these causes combine to exercise a very powerful influence on the conduct of the finances of the State. If the Americans never spend the people’s money on galas, it is not only because the imposition of taxes is under the people’s control, but because the people take no delight in public rejoicings. If they reject all ornament in their architecture and set store only on practical and homely advantages, it is not only because they live under democratic institutions, but because they are a commercial nation. The habits of private life carry over into public life, and we ought carefully to distinguish the economy that depends on their institutions from the economy that is the natural result of their customs.
Whether the Expenditure of the United States Can Be Compared to That of France

Two points must be established to estimate the extent of the public charges, namely the national wealth and the rate of taxation — The wealth and the charges of France are not accurately known — Why the wealth and charges of the Union cannot be accurately known — The author’s researches to discover the amount of taxation in Pennsylvania — General signs that may indicate the amount of the public charges in a given nation — Result of this investigation for the Union.

Many attempts have recently been made in France to compare the public expenditure of that country with that of the United States. All of them, however, have failed, and a few words will be enough to show that they could not have had a satisfactory result.

To estimate the amount of a people’s public charges, two preliminaries are indispensable. First, we must know the wealth of that people; second, we must learn what portion of that wealth goes to the expenditure of the State. To state the amount of taxation without stating the resources set aside to meet it is a futile labor, for what we want to know is not the expenditure, but the relation of the expenditure to the revenue.

The same rate of taxation that a wealthy contributor can easily bear will reduce a poor one to extreme misery. The wealth of nations is made up of several distinct elements, of which population is the first, real property the second, and personal property the third. The first of these can be discovered without difficulty. Among civilized nations it is easy to obtain an accurate census of the inhabitants; but the other two cannot be determined so easily. It is hard to take an exact account of all the lands in a country that are under cultivation, with their natural or acquired value; and it is still more impossible to estimate the entire personal property at a nation’s disposal, which eludes the strictest analysis through the variety and number of forms it can take. And indeed we find that the oldest civilized nations of Europe, even those with the most centralized administration, have not yet succeeded in determining the exact state of their wealth.

In America the attempt has never been made. How would such an investigation be possible in a country where society has not yet settled into habits of regularity and tranquility; where the national government is not assisted by a multitude of agents whose efforts it can command and direct to one single end; and where statistics are not studied, because no one is able to collect the necessary documents or to find time to read them? Thus the basic elements of the calculations made in France cannot be obtained in the Union. The relative wealth of the two countries is unknown; the property of the former is not accurately determined, and there is no means of computing that of the latter.

I therefore agree, for the sake of discussion, to abandon this necessary term of the comparison, and I confine myself to computing the actual amount of taxation, without investigating the relation between the taxation and the revenue. But the reader will see that the limits I set for my researches have not made my task any easier.

There can be no doubt that the central administration of France, assisted by all the public officers at its disposal, could determine exactly the amount of the direct and indirect taxes levied on the citizens. But this investigation, which no private individual can undertake, has not so far been completed by the French government, or at least its results have not been made public. We know the total sum of the charges of the State, and we know the amount of the departmental expenditure; but the expenses of the communal divisions have not been computed, and the amount of the public expenses of France is consequently unknown.

If we now turn to America, we find the difficulties multiplied and increased. The Union publishes an exact return of its expenditure; the budgets of the twenty-four States give similar returns of their revenues; but the expenses incurred in the affairs of the counties and the townships are unknown. *k

k [ The Americans, as we have seen, have four separate budgets: the Union, the States, the counties, and the townships each have their own. During my stay in America I made every effort to discover the amount of public expenditure in the townships and counties of the principal States of the Union. I readily obtained the budgets of the larger townships, but found it quite impossible to procure those of the smaller ones. I do possess some documents on county expenses which, although incomplete, are still curious. I have to thank Mr. Richards, Mayor of Philadelphia, for the budgets of thirteen of the counties of Pennsylvania, namely Lebanon, Centre, Franklin, Fayette, Montgomery, Luzerne, Dauphin, Butler, Alleghany, Columbia, Northampton, Northumberland, and Philadelphia, for the year 1830. Their population at that time consisted of 495,207 inhabitants. On looking at the map of Pennsylvania, it will be seen that these thirteen counties are scattered in every direction and so generally affected by the causes that usually influence the condition of a country that they may easily be supposed to give a correct average of the financial state of the counties of Pennsylvania in general. Thus, reckoning that the expenses of these counties in 1830 amounted to about $361,650, or nearly 75 cents for each inhabitant, and calculating that each inhabitant contributed in the same year about $2.55 to the Union and about 75 cents to the State of Pennsylvania, it appears that each contributed, as his share of all the public expenses (except those of the townships), the sum of $4.05. This calculation is doubly incomplete, since it applies only to a single year and to one part of the public charges; but it has at least the merit of not being conjectural.]

The authority of the Federal government cannot oblige the provincial governments to throw any light on this point; and even if those governments were willing to cooperate all together, it may be doubted that they have the means of giving a satisfactory answer. Apart from the natural difficulties of the task, the political organization of the country would hinder their efforts. The county and town magistrates are not appointed by the authorities of the State, and are not subject to their control. It is therefore quite reasonable to suppose that, if the State wanted to obtain the returns we require, its plan would be thwarted by the neglect of the subordinate officers it would have to employ. *l It is, in point of fact, useless to ask what the Americans might do to advance this inquiry, since it is certain that so far they have done nothing at all. There is not a single individual today, in America or in Europe, who can tell us what each citizen of the Union contributes each year to the public charges of the nation. *m [Footnote l: Those who have tried to compare the expenses of France and America have seen at once that no comparison could be drawn between the total expenditure of the two countries; but they have tried to contrast separate portions of this expenditure. It is easy to show that this second method is no less defective than the first. If I try to compare the French budget with the budget of the Union, it must be remembered that the latter covers far fewer objects than the central government of France, and that its expenditure must consequently be much smaller. If I contrast the budgets of the Departments with those of the States that make up the Union, it must be observed that, since the power and control exercised by the States are much greater than those exercised by the Departments, their expenditure is also greater. As for the budgets of the counties, nothing of the kind exists in the French system of finance; and it is again doubtful whether the corresponding expenses should be assigned to the budget of the State or to those of the municipal divisions. Municipal expenses exist in both countries, but they are not always analogous. In America the townships discharge a variety of offices that in France are reserved to the Departments or to the State. It may, moreover, be asked what is meant by the municipal expenses of America. The organization of the municipal bodies or townships differs from State to State. Are we to be guided by what happens in New England or in Georgia, in Pennsylvania or in the State of Illinois? A kind of analogy may easily be seen between certain budgets in the two countries; but since the elements that compose them always differ more or less, no fair comparison can be made between them. [The same difficulty exists, perhaps to a greater degree at the present time, when the taxation of America has largely increased. — 1874.]]

m [ Even if we knew the exact money contributions of every French and American citizen to the coffers of the State, we should come at only a portion of the truth. Governments demand not only supplies of money but also personal services, which may be regarded as equivalent to a given sum. When a State raises an army, besides the pay of the troops, which the entire nation provides, each soldier must give up his time, the value of which depends on the use he might make of it if he were not in the service. The same remark applies to the militia: the citizen in the militia devotes a certain portion of valuable time to maintaining the public peace, and in reality surrenders to the State the earnings he is prevented from making. Many other instances might be cited in addition to these. The governments of France and of America both levy taxes of this kind, which weigh on the citizens; but who can estimate accurately their relative amount in the two countries?

This, however, is not the last of the difficulties that prevent us from comparing the expenditure of the Union with that of France. The French government takes on certain obligations that do not exist in America, and vice versa. The French government pays the clergy; in America the voluntary principle prevails. In America there is a legal provision for the poor; in France they are left to public charity. French public officers are paid a fixed salary; in America they are allowed certain perquisites. In France contributions in kind are levied on very few roads; in America on almost all thoroughfares. In the former country the roads are free to all travelers; in the latter turnpikes abound. All these differences in the way contributions are levied in the two countries add to the difficulty of comparing their expenditure; for there are certain expenses that the citizens would not bear, or that would at any rate be much smaller, if the State did not take it upon itself to act in the name of the public.]

We must conclude, then, that it is no less difficult to compare the social expenditure than to estimate the relative wealth of France and America. I will even add that it would be dangerous to attempt the comparison; for when statistics are not based on strictly accurate computations, they mislead instead of guiding rightly. The mind is easily imposed on by the false show of exactness that prevails even in the misstatements of science, and it adopts with confidence errors dressed in the forms of mathematical truth.

We therefore abandon our numerical investigation, hoping to find data of another kind. In the absence of positive documents, we may form an opinion about the proportion between a people’s taxation and its real prosperity by observing whether its outward appearance is flourishing; whether, after meeting the demands of the State, the poor man keeps the means of subsistence and the rich man the means of enjoyment; and whether both classes are contented with their position, while seeking to improve it by constant exertion, so that industry is never short of capital, nor capital left unemployed by industry. An observer who draws his inferences from these signs will undoubtedly conclude that the American of the United States contributes a much smaller portion of his income to the State than the citizen of France. Nor, indeed, can the result be otherwise.

A portion of the French debt is the consequence of two successive invasions, and the Union has no similar calamity to fear. A nation located on the continent of Europe is obliged to maintain a large standing army; the isolated position of the Union lets it keep only 6,000 soldiers. The French have a fleet of 300 sail; the Americans have 52 vessels. *n How, then, can the inhabitants of the Union be called on to contribute as much as the inhabitants of France? No parallel can be drawn between the finances of two countries so differently situated.

n [ See the details in the Budget of the French Minister of Marine; and for America, the National Calendar of 1833, p. 228. [But the public debt of the United States in 1870, caused by the Civil War, amounted to $2,480,672,427, while that of France was more than doubled by the extravagance of the Second Empire and by the war of 1870.]]

It is by examining what actually happens in the Union, not by comparing the Union with France, that we can discover whether the American government is really economical. Looking over the different republics that make up the confederation, I see that their governments lack perseverance in their undertakings and exercise no steady control over the men they employ. From this I naturally infer that they must often spend the people’s money to no purpose, or use more of it than their undertakings really need. Great efforts are made, in keeping with the democratic origin of society, to meet the needs of the lower orders, to open the career of power to their efforts, and to spread knowledge and comfort among them. The poor are supported, immense sums are devoted every year to public instruction, all services of whatever kind are paid for, and the most subordinate agents are liberally paid. If this kind of government seems to me useful and rational, I am nevertheless compelled to admit that it is expensive.
Wherever the poor direct public affairs and dispose of the nation’s resources, it appears certain that, since they profit by the State’s expenditure, they tend to increase it.

I conclude, therefore, without resorting to inaccurate computations and without risking a comparison that might prove wrong, that the democratic government of the Americans is not a cheap government, as is sometimes claimed. And I have no hesitation in predicting that, if the people of the United States is ever involved in serious difficulties, its taxation will quickly be raised to the level that prevails in most of the aristocracies and monarchies of Europe. *o
o [ [That is precisely what has since occurred.]]
Corruption and Vices of the Rulers in a Democracy, and Consequent Effects Upon Public Morality

In aristocracies rulers sometimes try to corrupt the people — In democracies rulers often show themselves to be corrupt — In the former their vices directly harm the morality of the people — In the latter their indirect influence is still more pernicious.

A distinction must be made when the aristocratic and the democratic principles denounce each other as tending to encourage corruption. In aristocratic governments the individuals at the head of affairs are rich men who desire only power. In democracies statesmen are poor, and they have their fortunes to make. The consequence is that in aristocratic States the rulers are rarely open to corruption and have very little craving for money, while the reverse is the case in democratic nations.

But in aristocracies, since those who want to reach the head of affairs possess considerable wealth, and since the number of persons whose help they can use to rise is comparatively small, the government is, if I may use the expression, put up to a sort of auction. In democracies, on the contrary, those who covet power are very seldom wealthy, and the number of citizens who confer that power is extremely great. Perhaps in democracies the number of men who could be bought is by no means smaller, but buyers are rarely to be found; and besides, so many persons would have to be bought at once that the attempt is made futile.

Many of the men who have held office in France during the last forty years have been accused of making their fortunes at the expense of the State or of its allies, a reproach rarely made against the public figures of the ancient monarchy. But in France the practice of bribing electors is almost unknown, whereas in England it is notoriously and publicly carried on. In the United States I never heard a man accused of spending his wealth to corrupt the populace; but I have often heard the honesty of public officers questioned, and still more often I have heard their success attributed to low intrigues and immoral practices.

If, then, the men who run the government of an aristocracy sometimes try to corrupt the people, the heads of a democracy are themselves corrupt. In the first case the morality of the people is directly attacked; in the second an indirect influence is exercised on the people that is still more to be feared.

Since the rulers of democratic nations are almost always exposed to suspicion of dishonorable conduct, they in some measure lend the authority of the government to the base practices of which they are accused. They thus set an example that must discourage the struggles of virtuous independence and must feed the secret calculations of a vicious ambition. Someone may say that evil passions appear in all ranks of society, that they ascend the throne by hereditary right, and that despicable characters are to be found at the head of aristocratic nations as well as in the sphere of a democracy. This objection has little weight in my estimation. The corruption of men who have risen to power by chance has something coarse and vulgar about it that makes it contagious to the multitude. On the contrary, there is a kind of aristocratic refinement and an air of grandeur in the depravity of the great, which often keep it from spreading.

The people can never penetrate the bewildering labyrinth of court intrigue, and will always have difficulty detecting the baseness that lurks beneath elegant manners, refined tastes, and graceful language. But to plunder the public purse and to sell the favors of the State are arts that the meanest villain can understand and hope to practice in his turn.

In reality it is far less harmful to witness the immorality of the great than to witness the immorality that leads to greatness. In a democracy private citizens see a man of their own rank in life rise from that obscure position and come into riches and power within a few years. The sight excites their surprise and their envy, and they are led to ask how the person who was their equal yesterday is their ruler today. To attribute his rise to his talents or his virtues is unpleasant, for it is tacitly to acknowledge that they are themselves less virtuous and less talented than he was. They are therefore led (and not infrequently their guess is correct) to ascribe his success mainly to some one of his defects; and thus an odious mixture is formed in their minds of the ideas of baseness and power, unworthiness and success, utility and dishonor.
Efforts of Which a Democracy Is Capable

The Union has had only one struggle so far for its existence — Enthusiasm at the beginning of the war — Indifference toward its close — Difficulty of establishing military conscription or impressment of seamen in America — Why a democratic people is less capable of sustained effort than another.

I warn the reader here that I am speaking of a government that faithfully follows the real desires of a people, not of a government that simply commands in its name. Nothing is so irresistible as a tyrannical power commanding in the name of the people, because, while it exercises the moral influence that belongs to the decision of the majority, it acts at the same time with the promptness and tenacity of a single man.

It is difficult to say what degree of exertion a democratic government may be capable of in a crisis in the nation’s history. But no great democratic republic has so far existed in the world. To call the oligarchy that ruled France in 1793 by that name would be to insult the republican form of government. The United States offers the first example of the kind.

The American Union has now lasted half a century, and in all that time its existence has been attacked only once, namely during the War of Independence. At the beginning of that long war, various events showed an extraordinary zeal for the service of the country. *p But as the contest dragged on, signs of private egotism began to appear. No money was poured into the public treasury; few recruits could be raised for the army; the people wished to win independence but were very ill-disposed to undergo the privations by which alone it could be obtained. “Tax laws,” says Hamilton in the “Federalist” (No. 12), “have in vain been multiplied; new methods to enforce the collection have in vain been tried; the public expectation has been uniformly disappointed and the treasuries of the States have remained empty. The popular system of administration inherent in the nature of popular government, coinciding with the real scarcity of money incident to a languid and mutilated state of trade, has hitherto defeated every experiment for extensive collections, and has at length taught the different legislatures the folly of attempting them.”
